title: How Your Bond Amount Is Determined
excerpt: The bond amount is a multiple of your vehicle's value, set by your state. What differs between states is the multiplier and, more importantly, whose valuation they will accept.
metaDescription: How states calculate a title bond amount: the multiplier, accepted valuation methods like NADA and KBB, appraisals, and why the premium is a separate number.

body.text: Your bond amount is your vehicle's value multiplied by a figure your state sets, most often 1.5 or 2. What varies far more than the multiplier is whose valuation the state will accept, and getting that wrong is the most common reason an application is sent back.
The bond amount is coverage, not cost. It is the maximum the surety would pay a legitimate claimant. The premium is your cost: typically 1.5% of the bond amount, with a $100 minimum.

So a $10,000 vehicle in a state requiring 1.5x coverage needs a $15,000 bond, and that bond costs $225. You are not paying $15,000, and you never will unless a valid claim is made and you fail to reimburse the surety.
Broadly there are four accepted methods, and states pick one or allow a choice between several:

items: A national price guide such as NADA or Kelley Blue Book. Some states restrict this to vehicles under a certain age.
An appraisal by a licensed dealer, usually required on company letterhead and signed, sometimes with the dealer's licence number.
A state inspector's valuation, carried out as part of a vehicle inspection.
A schedule set by the state itself, based on vehicle type and age rather than an individual valuation.
Using a price guide in a state that requires a dealer appraisal, or for a vehicle older than the guide is accepted for.
Valuing the vehicle in its current condition when the state asks for retail value, or the reverse.
An appraisal that is missing the letterhead, the signature or the licence number the state asks for.
Rounding the bond amount down. States treat the required amount as a minimum.

body.text: A vehicle with no entry in any price guide needs one of the other routes, usually a dealer appraisal or a state inspection. The same applies to custom builds, kit vehicles and trailers assembled from parts, where there is no comparable model to price against.
Because every part of this is state-specific, check your state's page for its multiplier, its accepted valuation methods and its minimum bond amount before paying for a valuation.
